---
title: "Case study: 2625 Bedford Avenue"
subtitle: "City records flagged the construction site months before the building next door collapsed"
---

On November 11, 2026, the three-story building at **1321 Flatbush Avenue** in Brooklyn partially
collapsed, and at least one person died. It stood next to a construction site at
**2625 Bedford Avenue**, where a one-story building had been demolished. A DOB violation issued that
day attributes the collapse to "unsafe construction at 2625 Bedford Ave."

The public record shows warning signs at the construction site, not at the building that fell.

## Timeline from public records

| Date (2026) | Record | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Mar 11 | Construction fence permit issued for the site | DOB NOW permits |
| Mar 18 | Complaint: construction contrary to or beyond approved plans (category 83) | DOB complaints |
| ~Mar 20 | Stop-work order in place (dated from a later violation that cites site photos taken then) | ECB violations |
| Apr 23 | Class 1 violation, the most serious class, for continuing work while under a stop-work order; $10,000 penalty, later resolved | ECB violations |
| Sep | Earthwork and excavation-support permits issued | News reports (not independently checked) |
| Nov 10 | New fence permit, under a different contractor | DOB NOW permits |
| Nov 11 | Collapse; full stop-work orders, rear-yard vacates on adjoining lots, Class 1 violation for failing to safeguard | DOB and ECB violations |

## The building that collapsed

1321 Flatbush Avenue (four apartments, built 1930) had a long list of HPD violations the owner
never corrected, including Class C violations from August 2024 for sprinkler water supply,
self-closing doors and exposed wiring, and a leaking roof cited in 2022, 2024 and 2026. None
described cracks, bulging or settlement. Its only DOB violations before the collapse were from 2019,
for an advertising sign. No DOB complaints had been filed about it.

## What this case suggests

The strongest signal sat on the **adjacent lot**: a complaint about work beyond its permits, a
stop-work order that was ignored, then a contractor change, all next to an old masonry building in
poor repair. That points to a test the building-by-building approach misses: **construction
negligence on a neighboring lot**, weighted by the condition of the buildings around it.

::: {.caveat}
Investigators had not determined the cause at the time of writing. This page reports what public
records show; it does not assign fault. Records from NYC Open Data: DOB Violations (`3h2n-5cm9`),
ECB Violations (`6bgk-3dad`), DOB Complaints (`eabe-havv`), DOB NOW Permits (`rbx6-tga4`),
HPD Violations (`wvxf-dwi5`).
:::
